topics.chapterTitle: Designing Stable C++ APIs and Compatibility Boundaries
topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: An internal helper becomes a library. Another team links it into a service. A month later, a harmless-looking member change requires every consumer to rebuild, while an asynchronous callback occasionally reads a string that no longer exists. Neither problem is solved by documenting only the function names. A usable API must define ownership, lifetime, errors, and compatibility as carefully as it defines parameters.

topics.title: 3.1.1 Distinguishing Owned Values from Borrowed Views
topics.summary: An owned value carries responsibility for its storage. A borrowed view identifies storage owned elsewhere. std::string commonly expresses ownership; std::string_view expresses a nonowning view. Replacing a string with a view can remove a copy, but it can also move a lifetime obligation onto the caller. That is an API change even when ordinary examples continue to work.

topics.title: 3.1.2 Defining Valid States After Move and Shutdown
topics.summary: A moved-from object still exists. Its permitted operations depend on its contract. Many standard-library types promise a valid but unspecified state after a move, but that does not imply every user-defined type should allow every observer. A library should specify which operations remain meaningful rather than relying on callers to guess from an implementation detail.

topics.title: 3.2.1 Separating Rejection, Failure, and Uncertainty
topics.summary: A rejected request was not accepted because a known rule failed. A failed operation encountered a problem while attempting work. An uncertain outcome means the observer cannot determine whether the intended state transition occurred. Collapsing these into one Boolean forces callers to invent retry behavior without sufficient information.

topics.title: 3.2.2 Specifying Completion and Cancellation
topics.summary: A completion callback is an event with lifetime consequences. Specify whether it occurs exactly once for each successfully initiated operation, on which execution context it runs, and whether it may run inline before the initiating call returns. These choices affect reentrancy and ownership even when the actual computation is trivial.

blocks.text: Cancellation is usually a request to stop future or ongoing work, not a rollback of completed side effects. A cancelled caller may no longer want a result, while the remote system still needs to reconcile a committed job. A useful interface distinguishes caller interest, operation execution, and durable state rather than assigning them one flag.
rich: Cancellation is usually a request to stop future or ongoing work, not a rollback of completed side effects. A useful interface distinguishes caller interest, operation execution, and durable state rather than assigning them one flag.

blocks.text: Consider an operation object held by a shared_ptr. Capturing it in a completion handler can keep the state alive, but capturing the handler inside the object can also create an ownership cycle. Conversely, capturing this without retaining the owner can produce a use-after-free during shutdown. The interface should establish who owns completion state and when that ownership ends.

blocks.text: Completion order is another contract. A stream may preserve message order while several independent requests complete out of order. An API that exposes futures in submission order does not necessarily serialize remote effects. State the ordering scope and avoid promising more than the implementation enforces.

topics.title: 3.3.1 Understanding What Pimpl Hides and What It Does Not
topics.summary: The pointer-to-implementation idiom, or Pimpl, keeps private data layout out of a public header. A class can hold a pointer to a forward-declared implementation and define its destructor in a source file where the implementation is complete. Changing private fields can then avoid changing the visible class layout.

blocks.text: A superficial fix changes the capture to [&], which makes the problem worse by also borrowing the view variable itself. The correct repair is to choose an ownership contract: copy or move the payload into operation state, or require a caller-owned buffer whose lifetime is explicitly tied to completion. The first is usually easier for a general-purpose submission API; the second can be appropriate for specialized zero-copy interfaces with strong usage constraints.

blocks.text: Solution reasoning. An uncertain result should not manufacture a new key for the caller. Doing so can turn a retry into a second logical operation. The owned variant should retain its own buffer until completion. The borrowed variant must establish a completion event even after cancellation so the caller knows when reuse is safe. A statement that “cancellation usually stops it quickly” does not provide that lifetime guarantee.
